Winston Churchill. On June 4, 1940, just days after the British Expeditionary Force had been evacuated from Dunkirk, he addressed Parliament. Military prospects were bleak. Yet Churchill's words would crystallize the force of Britain's refusal to surrender and remain a touchstone of wartime leadership.

Churchill transformed catastrophe into victory. The Dunkirk evacuation could have been read as military disaster. Instead, he reframed the retreat as a successful deliverance of troops. Then he built his defiance in cascading waves: "We shall defend our island, whatever the cost may be, we shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets and in the hills." He employed biblical and classical rhetoric; the catalogue of resistance sites echoed ancient rallying cries. The speech concluded with an affirmation: "this shall be our finest hour."

Audiences reported being moved to tears. The speech became the emotional armor of the British public during the German threat. Later broadcast on radio, it amplified its reach beyond Parliament, becoming the sound of Britain's defiance. That steely resolve, first sounded in "Blood, Toil, Tears and Sweat" just weeks earlier, now reached its full rhetorical power.
